stubs.angle: A snippet assigns one struct variable to another, changes a field through the second variable and prints the field from both.
stubs.answerHinge: Assigning a struct copies all of its fields, so changing the copy leaves the original unchanged.

stubs.angle: A method receives a List<int> without ref, adds an item, then assigns a new list to the parameter, and the caller prints the count.
stubs.answerHinge: A reference is passed by value, so the caller sees a change made through the reference but not a reassignment of the parameter.

stubs.angle: Which of several statements that use an int variable performs boxing: assignment to object, widening to long, calling ToString, or List<int>.Add?
stubs.answerHinge: Boxing happens only when a value type is converted to object or an interface type; a numeric conversion, an overridden ToString call and a generic List<int> do not box.

stubs.angle: Is it true that value types live on the stack and reference types live on the heap, and where does an int field of a class instance actually live?
stubs.answerHinge: Where a value is stored depends on where the variable lives, not on its type: a value type field of a class, an array element or a captured local is stored on the heap inside the containing object.

stubs.angle: Select every value type among int, an enum, int[], string, a record struct and int?.
stubs.answerHinge: Enums, record structs and Nullable<T> are value types, while arrays are reference types even when their elements are value types.

stubs.angle: A snippet boxes an int into an object variable, then changes the int and prints both the object and the int.
stubs.answerHinge: Boxing copies the value into a new heap object, so later changes to the original variable do not affect the boxed copy.

stubs.angle: A class holds a mutable struct counter in a readonly field and calls its Increment method, but the printed count stays 0; find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: Calling a mutating method on a readonly field of a non-readonly struct operates on a defensive copy, so the field itself never changes.

stubs.angle: A snippet compares two struct instances with equal fields and two class instances with equal fields using Equals and prints both results.
stubs.answerHinge: ValueType.Equals compares the field values of structs, while object.Equals on a class without an override compares references.

stubs.angle: Which of several candidate types is the best fit for a struct according to the .NET framework design guidelines?
stubs.answerHinge: A struct fits a small (under about 16 bytes), immutable type that logically represents a single value and is rarely boxed; large, mutable or identity-bearing types should be classes.

stubs.angle: A snippet takes a Span<int> slice of an array, writes to the slice and prints the array.
stubs.answerHinge: Slicing a Span<T> creates a view over the same memory without copying, so writes through the slice change the underlying array.

stubs.angle: In C# 13 on .NET 9 or later, where may a Span<int> be used: a local in a synchronous method, a method parameter, a field of a ref struct, a field of a class, a List<Span<int>> element, a variable captured by a lambda?
stubs.answerHinge: Span<T> is a ref struct that must never escape to the heap, so it is allowed as a local, a parameter and a ref struct field, but not as a class field, a generic argument of List<T> or a captured variable.

stubs.angle: A snippet takes a ref local to a[0], assigns a new array to a, writes through the ref local and prints a[0] of the new array and of the saved old array.
stubs.answerHinge: A ref local aliases the storage location of the element in the original array object, not the variable a, so the write lands in the old array.

stubs.angle: A mutable struct implements ICounter; the snippet assigns it to an ICounter variable, calls Inc twice through the interface and once on the struct, then prints both counts.
stubs.answerHinge: Converting a struct to an interface boxes a copy, so interface calls mutate the box and direct calls mutate the original independently.

stubs.angle: A snippet boxes a null int? and an int? holding 5 into object variables and prints whether the first is null and the type name of the second.
stubs.answerHinge: Boxing a Nullable<T> without a value yields a null reference, and boxing one with a value yields a boxed T, never a boxed Nullable<T>.

stubs.angle: A 64-byte mutable struct is passed through several method layers in a hot loop; when does this cost more than a class, and what can reduce the cost?
stubs.answerHinge: Every pass and assignment copies the whole struct, so for large structs copying can outweigh the saved allocation; making it a readonly struct and passing it by in or ref removes copies and defensive copies.

stubs.angle: A parser must keep a reference to a slice of an input buffer in a class field and use it after an await; which type should hold the slice?
stubs.answerHinge: Memory<T> is not a ref struct and can live on the heap and across await, while Span<T> cannot, so the field should be Memory<T> and code converts it to Span<T> only for synchronous processing.

stubs.angle: A helper meant to skip a header row takes a List<string>.Enumerator parameter by value and calls MoveNext; the caller then loops over its own enumerator and still prints the header. Find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: List<T>.Enumerator is a mutable struct, so passing it by value copies its position; MoveNext advances only the copy, and the helper must take the enumerator by ref or work with IEnumerator<T>.

stubs.angle: A developer proposes converting many domain and DTO classes to structs to reduce allocations across the codebase; how do you decide and what rules do you set for the team?
stubs.answerHinge: Converting to structs changes semantics (copying, default values, equality, boxing) and can break public APIs, so allow it only for small immutable value-like types on measured hot paths, with benchmarks and review guidance rather than a blanket change.
